At the end of the old street, behind a wooden door that had grown tired of the seasons, the library waited. Nobody remembered when it first opened, or who had hung the brass lantern above its entrance.

Salim came in brushing the dust from his shoulder, and stood for a moment to listen. Libraries have a voice that only people who have lived among shelves can hear: the whisper of paper, the creak of timber, one long breath, as if the whole place were reading.
"You are late tonight," said the old man from behind the counter, without lifting his eyes from the ledger.
"The road was long," Salim answered, and then he smiled. "And the book you promised me is longer."

The old man closed the ledger slowly. He had the patience of a man who has watched many winters pass through the same window, and he did not hurry now. On the seventh shelf, he said, there was a volume that no one had borrowed in forty years, and no one had dared to put back.

Salim climbed the ladder one rung at a time. Each step answered with a different note, and by the fourth he had given up trying to be quiet. The seventh shelf smelled of cedar and rain, and between two thick atlases there was a gap exactly the width of a hand.
"It is not there," he called down.
"Of course it is not," the old man said. "It never stays where you look for it. Try looking for something else."
So Salim looked for a map instead, and the book fell open in his hands as if it had been waiting all along for someone to stop asking it questions.
The first page was blank. The second page held a single line in a hand he almost recognised: whoever finds this has already begun to read it.
